text.p: A controversy over a wealthy Indonesian businessman's campaign contributions to President Bill Clinton has led to "Asian-bashing" and selective scrutiny of the Asian-American community, civil rights leader Jesse Jackson charged on Monday.

Jackson, flanked by Asian Pacific American (APA) community leaders, told a news conference that people had been singled out by the news media and by "the Republican Party opposition research apparatus" for having Asian-sounding surnames.

"This is immigrant-bashing, Asian-bashing, is hypocrisy, is racism because it is of the worst of the so-called yellow peril that landed Japanese-Americans in intern camps in World War Two," Jackson said.

Jackson, on a nationwide "Get out the vote" drive in the final weeks of the presidential election campaign, called for campaign finance reform to halt the influence that big corporations apparently wield over both the Democratic Party and the Republican Party.
Republicans have questioned whether donations from individuals connected to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian banking and real estate business, had influenced administration policies.

The Lippo Group is one of Indonesia's biggest conglomerates and its deputy chairman James Riady, 39, is Clinton's friend. They met while Riady was working in a bank in Arkansas when Clinton was governor.

Jackson said that while he disagreed with the Clinton administration's Indonesian policies because he believed Jakarta violated human rights and international labour laws, he was alarmed by the intensity surrounding the Riady affair.
"I doubt that the same intensity would be exhibited were the suspected influence-peddlers British or Canadian rather than Asian or Asian-American," he said.

Clinton, well ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole in the opinion polls for the Nov. 5 election, has mentioned the fundraising uproar only once. But the Democratic National Committee was reviewing all donations to make sure they were appropriate.

"If there is some probable cause to call somebody then call them, we're looking at the selectivity based on Asian surnames," Jackson told reporters at the United States Information Agency's foreign press centre.
The APA said in a statement that the focus on Asian contributors "has a chilling effect on these communities as they exercise their legal right to participate in the American political process."
